[TODAY] We crashed into an asteroid. Now we're back. ☄️

In 2022, NASA's 580 kg DART spacecraft hit the small asteroid Dimorphos at 6.1 km/s, shortening its orbit around the bigger Didymos by about 33 minutes. ESA's Hera, about the size of a small car, now inspects the scene from 25 to 30 km away.

Didymos has gravity about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's, too weak for a normal orbit. Hera moves at 12 cm/s and fires its thrusters every few days, tracing rectangles around the pair.

Reality check: the big question, what the impact did to the asteroid itself, is still open. Detailed images come Nov. 25.

[TODAY] Built to last six years. It worked 27. 🛰️

NASA's Terra satellite, launched in December 1999, will stop collecting science data on Dec. 1. It was designed for a six-year mission and kept going more than four times that long.

Over a quarter century, Terra tracked land use, wildfires, dust and smoke, air quality and ice cover. Its data informed decisions on public safety, farming and water.

Reality check: its systems are aging and its orbit is drifting. The team will use leftover fuel to lower it, then power it off in January 2027. Its data records stay free to the public.

[TODAY] This star exploded about 50 million years ago. 💥

Why only now? Light takes time to travel. Supernova SN 2026ahvu sits in the galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years away, so the light reaching us left about 50 million years ago. The ATLAS survey spotted it on Nov. 2.

It is a Type Ia supernova: a white dwarf, the dense core of a dead star, blew itself apart. This kind peaks at a predictable brightness, so astronomers use it to measure cosmic distances.

Reality check: the distance is an estimate. It should peak between Nov. 18 and 23, in the southern constellation Horologium.

Save this for the next starlight debate.

[TODAY] A star swallowed its partner in seven years. ⭐

In our neighbor galaxy Andromeda, a star of about 0.7 times the Sun's mass spiraled into a puffy supergiant 350 times the Sun's radius. Once they touched, the merger took only about seven orbits, roughly seven years. Other known mergers took thousands of orbits.

NASA's Webb telescope looked just 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest follow-up of such an event. The study appeared in Nature on Nov. 18.

Reality check: what the merged star turns into is still unknown.

[IMAGINE] Over €100 million to catch one dead satellite. 🛰️

What is real: on Nov. 17, ESA signed a contract worth more than €102 million with OHB to lead ClearSpace-1. The servicer will find ESA's 95 kg PROBA-1 satellite, launched in 2001, grab it and steer both down for a controlled reentry. PROBA-1 was never built to be caught, so the approach must be largely autonomous.

Reality check: OHB says launch is planned for 2030 (ESA's mission page still lists 2029). Thousands of dead satellites already orbit Earth.

The speculation: what if one day orbit had a fleet of tow trucks clearing old satellites?
